cognitive_definition: Availability heuristic: people judge how frequently or probably an event occurs by how easily they can recall examples of it; events just experienced disproportionately influence later judgments.
core_case: Because Tang Sanzang had just been deceived by the White Bone Demon, he thereafter presumed that any beautiful woman or old man was a demon — a textbook case of availability bias.

tang_monk_evolution.characteristic: Trusts all beings and is unwilling to take life
tang_monk_evolution.representative_event: Wukong kills the Six Robbers; Tang Sanzang is furious
tang_monk_evolution.key_quote: We are monastics; do not take any life

tang_monk_evolution.phase: Turning Point · the White Bone Demon
tang_monk_evolution.characteristic: The White Bone Demon's three transformations (maiden / old woman / old man) successfully deceive Tang Sanzang; Wukong is banished
tang_monk_evolution.representative_event: Thrice Beats the White Bone Demon; Tang Sanzang chants the Golden Hoop Mantra and banishes Wukong
tang_monk_evolution.cognitive_bias: First establishes the belief that 'a beautiful woman may be a demon'
tang_monk_evolution.key_quote: You monkey, you are plainly killing and destroying life

tang_monk_evolution.characteristic: Presumes any beautiful woman or old man is a demon; over-suspicious
tang_monk_evolution.representative_event: Red Boy turns into a child; Tang Sanzang believes him
tang_monk_evolution.cognitive_bias: Availability bias, but reversed: he doubts only Wukong, never others
tang_monk_evolution.key_quote: If there is a demon, Wukong, you must strike it down

tang_monk_evolution.characteristic: After many episodes, begins to trust Wukong's judgment
tang_monk_evolution.representative_event: After the Red Boy incident, Tang Sanzang gradually trusts Wukong
tang_monk_evolution.cognitive_bias: Availability bias corrected, but still occasionally flares up
tang_monk_evolution.key_quote: Wukong, tell me — is it a demon or not?

comparative_cases.case: The White Bone Demon's three transformations
comparative_cases.consequence: Wukong is banished; Tang Sanzang meets the Yellow Robe Demon

comparative_cases.case: Red Boy turns into a child
comparative_cases.cognitive_error: Failed to learn from the White Bone Demon; still over-trusting
comparative_cases.consequence: Tang Sanzang is captured; Wukong seeks Guanyin's help

comparative_cases.case: Gold Horn and Silver Horn transform
comparative_cases.consequence: Wukong sees through them; danger turns to safety

comparative_cases.case: The ghost of the Black Rooster Kingdom's king

comparative_cases.tang_monk_judgment: Believes she is a virtuous maiden
comparative_cases.cognitive_error: Bias still not fully corrected even late in the journey
comparative_cases.consequence: Tang Sanzang is captured; Wukong seeks Heavenly King Li's help

cognitive_insights: Tang Sanzang's availability bias is 'reversed': he never doubts strangers, only Wukong
The White Bone Demon episode is the cognitive turning point, but Tang Sanzang's misattribution (blaming Wukong) reinforced the bias
Availability bias leaves Tang Sanzang's judgment error rate at 60% even late in the journey
Tang Sanzang's cognitive correction is extremely slow; even by Chapter 80 it is still incomplete
Wukong's Fiery Golden Eyes are a cognitive tool, but Tang Sanzang distrusts the tool — the root of the cognitive conflict
